title: Verifier‑Grounded Generate‑Verify‑Repair for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Paired Mininet Emulation Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents; 400 paired episodes) to evaluate whether a deterministic verifier‑grounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces operationally detectable policy‑violation errors when a hosted LLM produces device configuration sequences from operator intent in a Mininet emulation. Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one sampled initial generation per intent reused by both baseline and guarded). Baseline success (no detected policy violation) = 196/200 (98%); guarded success = 200/200 (100%). Paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.02; preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory test). An exploratory paired bootstrap (seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) yields a 95% percentile CI = [0.005, 0.04]. Four verifier‑triggered repairs occurred (total hosted model calls = 204), giving mean extra model calls per intent = 0.02 and mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0. All reported numeric values, provider‑call accounting, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are drawn verbatim from the archived execution and analysis bundle. We interpret the preregistered confirmatory result conservatively and discuss construct, internal, and external validity limits and operational implications.

sections.introduction:
Automating natural‑language intent→device‑configuration translation promises to reduce operator effort in NetOps, but large language models (LLMs) can produce mechanically detectable faults—syntax errors, reachability/topology violations, and ACL/policy mistakes—that may have operational consequences (outages, unintended access) [1], [4]. A pragmatic mitigation pattern is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline: a model produces a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks mechanizable constraints, and, if violations are found, the model is asked to repair using localized diagnostic feedback [2], [3]. Prior prototypes show verifier‑grounded repair reduces mechanically checkable errors in code and domain‑specific program generation, but questions remain about scaling GVR across heterogeneous vendor templates, concrete hosted‑LLM cost per avoided policy violation, and correct interpretation of paired comparisons when a shared initial candidate is reused across conditions.

We preregistered study C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 to address these gaps with a confirmatory paired design executed in Mininet emulation. Key design features (frozen before any model calls) include: deterministic stratified sampling across three synthetic vendor‑template families and four topology patterns, explicit shared_initial_candidate sampling semantics (one sampled candidate per intent reused by both baseline and guarded conditions), a deterministic validator that checks syntactic, sequencing, reachability, and encoded ACL/policy constraints, and a bounded repair policy allowing at most one verifier‑triggered repair per intent. The primary estimand compares the per‑intent probability of zero operationally detectable violations under guarded (GVR) versus baseline (single‑shot) generation using an exact McNemar two‑sided test. All execution, model‑call accounting, and validator traces are archived and reported verbatim from the execution manifest.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and NetOps‑specific analyses document rapid growth in LLM‑for‑NetOps work and recurring evaluation gaps: benchmark provenance, verifier integration, and limited multi‑vendor emulation evidence [5], [6]. Prototype studies demonstrate that LLMs can draft device configurations but often introduce syntax/topology or policy errors; verifier‑guided repair appears repeatedly as a mitigation strategy in code and domain‑program generation [2], [3]. NetConfEval and related benchmarks illustrate potential for intent→configuration evaluation but remain task‑limited and often lack provenance‑traced closed‑loop verifier pipelines [4].

Our study extends these lines by (i) applying a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory design across heterogeneous synthetic templates in an emulator, (ii) executing and documenting shared_initial_candidate semantics so paired differences derive only from deterministic validator/repair actions, and (iii) reporting complete provider and verifier accounting to quantify concrete hosted‑LLM cost per avoided violation. We intentionally avoid claims of production readiness; the contribution is an artifact‑grounded proof‑of‑concept under tightly specified scope.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered as C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 before any model calls (preregistration SHA‑256 = 9e0fc992665835975b01289f7841926ef6abf3584252c5d0459ba0ecf166bb50). The primary confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (probability that an intent yields zero operationally detectable violations under guarded minus baseline) tested with an exact McNemar two‑sided test (α = 0.05). Predeclared exploratory summaries include a paired bootstrap percentile CI for the risk difference (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) and cost metrics (mean extra hosted model calls per intent; mean extra calls per avoided violation).

Sampling, strata, and shared_initial_candidate semantics: N = 200 unique operator intents were deterministically selected and stratified across three vendor‑template families and four topology patterns (12 strata) using the frozen task_index_profile. Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial sampled generation per intent was produced and reused by both baseline and guarded episodes. Under this semantics, baseline outcome equals the validator verdict on that shared initial candidate; guarded outcome equals the final guarded pipeline result after deterministic validation and any permitted repair. The preregistration explicitly declared that independent constrained‑prompt arms were not executed; the comparison therefore isolates validator/repair effects only.

Model configuration and temperature notation: Archived execution artifacts declare the model as gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). The model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; we state explicitly that null/unset is not evidence of deterministic provider sampling and does not imply temperature = 0.

Deterministic validator and repair policy: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performs syntactic parsing, required‑command sequencing checks, reachability/topology verification against the emulated network state, and encoded ACL/policy checks derived from the task payload constraints. The validator emits a boolean success = "no detected violations" under the scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation. The guarded pipeline allowed up to one verifier‑triggered repair call per intent; repair prompts were constructed from the validator's localized diagnostics and issued only when the validator reported violations. Validator traces (validation_before and validation_after) and any repair decisions are archived per episode.

Scoring, exclusions, and analysis plan: The primary analysis is an exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary success indicators. Exclusion rules and missingness treatments were preregistered: duplicate tasks (detected by deterministic hashing), unrecoverable infrastructure failures, or container/template substitution failures would be excluded and reported. Ambiguous validator outputs are conservatively treated as violations in the primary analysis. In execution no pairs were excluded and no episodes failed. Sensitivity analyses were predeclared to treat infrastructure failures conservatively as failures if present.

Deterministic accounting: The execution_manifest records hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 decomposed as 200 shared_initial_generation events and 4 repair calls (cache_hit_count = 0; cache_miss_count = 204). Stage accounting reports shared_initial_generation = 200 and repair stage = 4. These audited counts are reported verbatim in Results to enable reconciliation with archived artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution completeness and contingency: The run completed as preregistered: planned_episode_count = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; complete_pair_count = 200; failed_episode_count = 0. The paired 2×2 contingency (guarded vs baseline success) is: n11 = 196 (both succeed), n10 = 4 (guarded succeed, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline succeed), n00 = 0 (both fail). Baseline success rate = 196/200 = 0.98; guarded success rate = 200/200 = 1.0; paired point estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.02.

Confirmatory hypothesis test and exploratory interval: The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test on the paired binary outcomes yields p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory result; do not reject at α = 0.05). The archived exploratory paired bootstrap (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) produced a 95% percentile CI for the paired risk difference = [0.005, 0.04]. Both the exact test result and the bootstrap computation (seed and resamples) are archived and reported verbatim; the McNemar exact test is the formal confirmatory inference per the preregistration. We caution that when discordant pair counts (n10 + n01) are small, resampling intervals can be unstable and should be considered exploratory magnitude indicators rather than confirmatory evidence.

Repair and provider cost accounting: Four verifier‑triggered repairs were invoked across the 200 intents. Total hosted model calls = 204 (200 shared initial + 4 repair calls), yielding mean hosted model calls per intent = 1.02 and mean extra calls per intent = 0.02. Each repair corrected one baseline failure in the archived contingency; thus mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0. These arithmetic derivations are direct from the audited provider_call counts in the execution_manifest.

Representative artifact diagnostics: Representative per‑episode validator traces (e.g., execution/scoring/task‑000004‑*.json entries) show identical shared_initial_candidate content and identical baseline and guarded shared_initial responses (the shared initial text was reused by both conditions). For the four discordant pairs, validator_trace.validation_before recorded detected violations and repair prompts were issued; validator_trace.validation_after recorded that repairs were applied and the final configurations were valid under full_intent_constraint_validation. These per‑episode artifacts substantiate the contingency table and repair accounting reported above.

Statistical power context: The preregistered power plan targeted detection of a 10 percentage point absolute reduction with N ≈ 157 (McNemar approximation) and selected N = 200 to allow stratified description. The observed baseline failure prevalence (2%) was lower than some planning scenarios, reducing power to detect small absolute improvements and explaining the non‑significant McNemar result despite a positive point estimate. This sensitivity between assumed baseline prevalence and realized prevalence is an important consideration for future study planning.
sections.discussion:
Inference under shared_initial_candidate semantics: Because the execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one sampled initial generation per intent reused by baseline and guarded), any paired improvement derives solely from deterministic validator/repair actions rather than from independent first‑pass re‑sampling, prompt changes, or constrained‑prompt arms (those arms were not executed). The preregistration explicitly declared this execution semantics and the deterministic_reconciliation verifies it in the archived manifest. Readers should therefore interpret the guarded–baseline paired difference as the causal effect of permitting deterministic validation and up to one repair call on the exact same initial model candidate.

Operational implications (artifact‑grounded and bounded): In this Mininet emulation with synthetic provenance‑traced templates and a validator that expresses relevant template constraints, a small repair budget (four repairs) eliminated the mechanically detectable baseline violations for this workload at low model‑call overhead (mean extra calls per intent = 0.02). This suggests that when a suitable deterministic verifier exists and provides localized diagnostic feedback, bounded repair budgets can remove mechanically checkable faults in template‑driven emulated settings. These findings do not establish production readiness: they do not measure production hardware effects, other LLMs, prompt families, or semantic errors outside the validator's rule set.

Threats to validity: Construct validity—the validator covers syntactic, sequencing, reachability, and encoded ACL/policy checks but cannot detect higher‑order semantic misinterpretations not expressible in its rules. Internal validity—shared_initial_candidate semantics were executed as preregistered and audited, preventing attribution of observed gains to between‑condition sampling differences. Conclusion validity—small discordant counts limit power and make resampling estimates less stable; the exact McNemar test is therefore appropriate for confirmatory inference. External validity—single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), synthetic templates, and Mininet emulation limit generalization to production devices, other models, or different prompt/adapter designs.

Recommendations grounded in the archived evidence: (1) Extend deterministic verifier coverage to express richer semantic/policy ontologies and measure residual false negatives empirically; (2) run paired designs that compare shared_initial_candidate semantics with independent multi‑sample initial generations to isolate prompt/template effects (not executed here); (3) evaluate multiple hosted models and provider versions to assess robustness to provider nondeterminism; (4) preserve provenance tracing for all provider calls and validator traces to enable independent audit. Each recommendation follows directly from observed artifacts and documented limitations.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents; shared_initial_candidate semantics) to measure whether a deterministic verifier plus bounded repair reduces mechanically detectable policy violations for intent→configuration tasks in a Mininet emulation. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test did not reject at α = 0.05 (p = 0.125). Guarded GVR invoked four repairs and corrected the four observed baseline violations at low model‑call overhead (mean extra calls per intent = 0.02), yielding a paired risk difference estimate of 0.02 and an exploratory paired bootstrap CI = [0.005, 0.04] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). When a deterministic verifier can express and check relevant constraints and provide localized feedback, a small repair budget can eliminate mechanically detectable policy violations in similar template‑based emulated settings. The results do not establish production readiness, multi‑model generality, or coverage for semantic errors outside the validator. Future preregistered, provenance‑traced evaluations should expand verifier coverage, evaluate multiple hosted models, and compare independent multi‑sample baselines.

Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Preregistration: C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 (SHA‑256 = 9e0fc992665835975b01289f7841926ef6abf3584252c5d0459ba0ecf166bb50) was recorded before any model calls. Sampling semantics: execution used shared_initial_candidate (exactly one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and reused by both baseline and guarded); archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset (null/unset is not evidence of deterministic provider sampling and does not imply temperature = 0). Provider accounting (audited): hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 decomposed as 200 shared initial generations + 4 repair calls. Reported numbers and analysis artifacts are drawn from the archived execution and analysis bundles.
limitations: Scope limited to Mininet‑style emulation with synthetic, provenance‑traced intent→configuration tasks; results do not generalize directly to production hardware or live operations.
Single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) evaluated; multi‑model generality is not established.

Deterministic validator coverage limited to mechanically checkable errors (syntax, reachability, ACL/policy encodings); higher‑level semantic or specification misinterpretations outside the validator may remain undetected.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics imply observed paired differences derive only from verifier‑triggered repair; this design does not measure effects of alternative prompting strategies or independent multi‑sample candidate selection.

Observed confirmatory effect (2 percentage points) did not reach statistical significance at α = 0.05 for N = 200 (exact McNemar p = 0.125); low baseline failure prevalence (2%) reduced power to detect small absolute improvements under some preregistered scenarios.
